explanation: Israeli traffic regulations cap a commercial vehicle's overall width at 2.55 meters, since a wider vehicle would need extra lane clearance; vehicles with refrigeration units get a special exception for their added wall insulation.

A 'Caution, wide load' sign must be displayed once a load's width passes 2.50 meters, because at that width the cargo overhangs the vehicle enough to surprise or endanger other drivers if it isn't flagged.

Drivers of vehicles over 6,000 kg are limited to a maximum of 4 hours of continuous driving before a half-hour rest, since fatigue builds with driving time and lengthens reaction time in heavy vehicles that already need more stopping distance.
Vehicle-dimension regulations set 18.75 meters as the maximum overall length allowed for this class of vehicle, beyond which maneuverability and lane-keeping on public roads become unsafe.
The regulations cap a three-axle commercial vehicle at 12.00 meters overall length to keep it maneuverable on standard roads and at junctions.
A two-axle commercial vehicle is likewise limited to 12.00 meters overall length under the vehicle-dimension regulations.
The pictured sign is a guidance/information sign marking the entrance to a city, settlement, or regional center, distinct from parking, shooting-range, or train-station markers that look different.
'Permitted load' refers specifically to the maximum weight in kilograms that may legally be loaded onto the vehicle, separate from the vehicle's own weight or its total all-up weight.

For vehicles over 15,000 kg, freight may overhang the rear by up to one third of the loading platform's length, but only when it is carried as a single undivided unit, since a divided load is harder to secure and predict on the road.
A multi-axle trailer built to carry containers of any size must have an all-up weight of not less than 29,000 kg, reflecting the heavy loads such containers impose on the structure.

A driver whose health changes in a way that could affect fitness to drive must report it immediately to the Licensing Bureau by registered mail, since driving fitness is a condition the Licensing Authority continuously monitors.
Freight wider than 3.40 meters requires a police officer's permit before it can be transported, since such an oversize load poses a hazard to other road users that needs official oversight.
Freight rising more than 4.80 meters above the ground generally requires a police officer's approval, matching the standard low-clearance threshold used on overpass warning signs.

For a heavy vehicle over 15,000 kg all-up weight, the law allows a single-unit load up to 4.80 meters high without a special police permit, reflecting the higher clearance such vehicles are built for.
Vehicles with an all-up weight between 8,000 and 15,000 kg may carry freight up to 4.00 meters high without extra permits, a lower ceiling than for heavier vehicles.
A flashing yellow lamp above the driver's compartment is required once the vehicle or its freight exceeds 20 meters in length, warning other drivers of the unusually long combination ahead.
A bus's registration cannot be issued or renewed more than 20 years after its manufacture date, since aging buses pose greater mechanical and safety risks when carrying passengers.

A pedestrian crossing is a priority zone for pedestrians, so even though another driver already slowed, you must not assume the pedestrian will watch out for you; you must slow down and let them finish crossing safely.
Drivers of commercial vehicles over 6,000 kg are legally entitled to at least 52 rest days per year, a fixed minimum meant to counter the fatigue risks of professional heavy-vehicle driving.

Drivers of public service vehicles and of commercial vehicles over 6,000 kg approved for at least 11 passengers must rest at least 7 consecutive hours before starting a work day, since fatigue is especially dangerous when many passengers are at risk.
The depicted flashing orange light is a temporary warning used at road works, distinguishing it from the fixed, constant signals used at junctions or malfunctioning traffic lights.
Carrying a freight container requires a commercial motor vehicle with a minimum all-up weight of 16,000 kg, since containers are heavy loads that only a sufficiently robust vehicle is built to bear.

An escort is required for oversize freight once its width exceeds 3.40 meters, the same width threshold at which a police permit is also mandated, because such a wide load can't safely share the road unassisted.

A trailer or semi-trailer that has no floor or walls needs chains and flags (perimeter lighting) marking its outline, since without a solid body its actual dimensions and load aren't otherwise visible to other drivers.
The law exempts only private passenger cars, tractors, motorcycles, and motorcycle-with-sidecar combinations from carrying a fire extinguisher; every other motor vehicle must have one.
A trailer must have an all-up weight of at least 15,000 kg to be approved for carrying a container, ensuring the trailer's structure can bear that kind of load.

Responsibility for arranging the freight securely and keeping it intact rests with the driver alone, since the driver is the one in control of the vehicle and accountable for how it is loaded during the trip.

Both the driver and the vehicle owner share responsibility for keeping the speed governor in proper working order, since the device exists to enforce a legal speed limit that both parties are accountable for maintaining.

Transporting high freight needs police-officer approval specifically when the vehicle's all-up weight exceeds 15,000 kg and the freight rises above 4.80 meters, the same clearance threshold used elsewhere for oversize-height permits.

Only a police officer is authorized to grant permission for oversize freight on a vehicle over 15,000 kg, since assessing road and traffic safety for such a load is a policing function, not an administrative one.

A 6.10-meter container must be loaded on the rear part of a semi-trailer, and only when proper twist locks are fitted, since those locks are what secure the container to the chassis and prevent it shifting.

Tires and brakes still need distance and time to overcome the vehicle's momentum, so during an emergency stop the vehicle continues traveling some distance before coming to a complete stop rather than stopping instantly.

A rescue and towing vehicle up to 16,000 kg may not have its registration issued or renewed more than 19 years after its manufacture date, limiting how long an aging vehicle in this heavy-duty role stays in service.
A commercial vehicle up to 3,500 kg may carry freight no higher than 3.0 meters above the road surface, a lower ceiling suited to this lighter vehicle class.
A commercial vehicle up to 8,000 kg may carry freight up to 3.50 meters above the road surface, one tier higher than the 3,500 kg class.

Before making a U-turn on a straight section, the driver must confirm the turn isn't being made just before a hill, since a hill crest would block the sightline needed to see oncoming traffic in time.
The flashing yellow lamp above a truck's driver's compartment becomes obligatory once the freight's width exceeds 3 meters, marking the vehicle as carrying an unusually wide load.

'Overall height' is measured from the road surface to the vehicle's highest point, including all its fixtures, while the vehicle is unloaded, giving a consistent baseline figure for the vehicle itself.

'All up weight' is defined as the vehicle's own weight plus the weight of everyone and everything it is approved by the Licensing Authority to carry, giving the total legal weight ceiling for that vehicle.

'Own weight' means the vehicle's weight complete with all its accessories, fuel, water, and oil, but excluding the driver and any freight, representing the vehicle in its ready-to-drive but unloaded state.
A 'desert vehicle' is a public vehicle with both front- and rear-wheel drive and a standard chassis that is specifically designated as such in its registration document.
In this basic legal sense, a 'commercial vehicle' is simply any motor vehicle that is used or designed to carry goods.

Work vehicles and commercial vehicles over 12,000 kg are limited to 50 km/h in urban areas and 80 km/h on any other type of road, a lower ceiling than for lighter vehicles because of their size and stopping distance.

The 110 km/h freeway limit doesn't apply to commercial vehicles over 12,000 kg, work vehicles, touring vehicles, or other 'slow moving' vehicles, since their handling and stopping distances make that speed unsafe for them.
Driving a commercial vehicle under 12,000 kg all-up weight requires a C1 license, the license class set for medium-weight goods vehicles.
Driving a commercial vehicle over 12,000 kg all-up weight requires a C license, the class reserved for heavier goods vehicles than those covered by C1.
Towing a 4,000 kg trailer with a commercial vehicle over 3,500 kg requires a C+E license, since combining a heavy vehicle with a heavy trailer needs the combined-vehicle license class.
Sign 216 is the specific sign that marks the start of a freeway (fast/express road), distinct from the other numbered signs in that series which mark different stages or types of restricted roads.
Here, a 'commercial vehicle' is defined more precisely as one used or designed to carry freight for hire, or to serve the purpose of its owner's occupation, distinguishing it from a private vehicle.
A 'work vehicle' is one fitted with work equipment and not designed to carry freight or transport passengers, distinguishing it from ordinary commercial or passenger vehicles.
A trailer over 4,000 kg all-up weight must carry an additional license plate mounted on its rear, so the trailer itself remains identifiable independent of the towing vehicle.
Vehicles over 150 cm wide must carry two red-and-yellow reflective plates on the rear wall, with a red outer frame, so the vehicle's full width is visible to traffic approaching from behind at night.
A commercial vehicle over 12,500 kg must be marked with two light-reflecting plates at the rear, making its bulk and position visible to following traffic in low light.

On a semi-trailer, the gap between the cab and the trailer's front wall must allow both to move freely in every direction, including full movement of the connecting air pipes, without the two parts touching even during the sharpest turn.
The 'fifth wheel' is the plate-shaped fixture that connects the cab (truck tractor) to the semi-trailer, forming the pivot point that lets the trailer turn relative to the cab.

Vehicle headlights are required to illuminate the road with a uniform white or bright-yellow light, ensuring consistent visibility rather than patchy or colored lighting that could confuse other drivers.

The chains linking a towing vehicle to its trailer must be strong and long enough to allow the trailer to swing through a 90-degree turn or more relative to the tow vehicle without breaking or restricting the connection.

The gap between the rear of the towing vehicle and the front of the trailer must not exceed 150 cm, keeping the combination compact and stable while still allowing the connecting components to function.

A commercial vehicle needs a towing permit to pull a trailer once its own all-up weight exceeds 10,000 kg, since combining two heavy units changes the handling and braking demands enough to require official approval.
The fire-extinguisher requirement covers every motor vehicle except private passenger cars, tractors, and motorcycles, since those excluded types are judged lower fire risk or impractical to equip.

A trailer or semi-trailer wider than 120 cm that has no floor or walls and is built for carrying long freight must have chains or cables and lamps during lighting-up time, since its true outline wouldn't otherwise be visible to other drivers in the dark.
Safety shoes are mandatory in every motor vehicle over 5,000 kg all-up weight, except buses, reflecting the greater physical risks involved in operating and loading heavier commercial vehicles.

Any motor vehicle over 3,500 kg, plus buses and work vehicles, must show distress lights or a flashing yellow lamp if forced to stop on a non-urban road during lighting-up time, so its stationary bulk is visible to approaching traffic in the dark.

The yellow flashing light of a portable warning lamp must be visible from 150 meters away in good weather during lighting-up time, giving approaching drivers enough distance to react to a stopped vehicle.
A speed governor is mandatory on vehicles over 12,000 kg, truck tractors, and work vehicles, since these heavier or more powerful vehicles need a hard cap on speed to prevent loss of control.

Mud protectors are required on every vehicle whose rear wheels aren't already covered by wings, except tractors and speed-restricted vehicles, to stop debris and water being thrown at following traffic.

A low rear collision-protection bumper is required on commercial vehicles, trailers, semi-trailers, and work vehicles over 3,500 kg, to prevent smaller vehicles from sliding underneath in a rear-end collision.
The legal definition of a 'public service vehicle' is one used or designed to transport passengers for hire, covering any vehicle built or used for that commercial passenger-carrying purpose.

A third license plate is required on trucks fitted with reclining/tilting trailers, since the extra plate keeps the vehicle identifiable when the trailer's configuration differs from a standard fixed trailer.

A reverse-drive buzzer is mandatory on commercial and work vehicles over 15,000 kg, as well as on tractors and buses, since their size creates larger blind spots that make an audible reversing warning necessary.

Extremity (width) side lights are required once a vehicle is 210 cm wide or more, so its full width is visible to other drivers at night, since a wider vehicle needs a clearer outline than standard lights alone provide.
Parking lights are not required on a vehicle that already has extremity (width) side lights fitted, since those side lights already serve the function parking lights would otherwise provide.

An independent brake is mandatory on trailers and semi-trailers with an all-up weight of 8,000 kg or more, since a trailer that heavy needs its own reliable braking rather than depending solely on the towing vehicle.

An ABS anti-lock braking system is mandatory on commercial vehicles with an all-up weight of 12,000 kg or more, since heavier vehicles benefit most from ABS's ability to prevent wheel lock-up and preserve steering control during hard braking.

A compression brake (retarder) is required on commercial and work vehicles weighing 8,000 kg or more, since a vehicle that heavy needs an auxiliary braking system to control speed safely on long descents without overheating the main brakes.

'Service brakes' refers to the main braking system that acts on all the vehicle's wheels and is designed to slow or stop the vehicle in any road condition, as distinct from an auxiliary or parking brake.

An 'independent brake' is a spring-loaded braking device that automatically engages if the air pressure in the braking system drops below the required level, acting as a fail-safe rather than a brake the driver operates directly.
A 'speed retarder' is an electric or hydraulic mechanism separate from the vehicle's regular braking system that slows the vehicle down when engaged, typically used to control speed on long descents.

A 'pedestrian crossing' is legally defined as a section of roadway specifically designated, by markings or a traffic sign, to permit pedestrians to cross, distinguishing it from any spot where people just happen to cross.

The Licensing Authority can permit a vehicle exceeding standard size and weight regulations, but only under special conditions, since some exceptional loads genuinely require an exemption from the normal limits.

When parking downhill, the driver must turn the front wheels toward the sidewalk and shift into reverse gear (or 'P' in an automatic), so that if the parking brake fails, the vehicle rolls into the curb rather than out into traffic.
The pictured sign marks the end of a taxi rank, not its start, so it tells drivers the taxi-only restriction that applied further back no longer applies at that point.

Approaching a high point or any spot where the view ahead is blocked, a driver must slow to a speed matching how far they can actually see, since driving faster than your sightline allows means you couldn't stop in time for a hidden hazard.

From November 1st each year, every commercial vehicle over 10,000 kg must carry a certificate showing it passed a winter check or annual test done in August or later, ensuring the vehicle is verified roadworthy heading into winter.
A vehicle of 16,000 kg or more must have its braking system checked at least once every half year, reflecting the greater wear and greater consequences of brake failure on the heaviest vehicles.
An 'axle' is the shaft or system of drive shafts running across the width of the vehicle on which a set of wheels is mounted, the basic structural unit used to count a vehicle's wheel sets.

Sign 403 specifically marks a level (railway) crossing that has a barrier, telling the driver to stop when that barrier is down or closing, unlike the other numbered signs which cover different crossing or road types.
'Gross axle weight' is the total weight pressing down on the road from all the wheels mounted on a single axle, distinct from the axle's own structural weight.

Unprescribed medications can impair driving just as much as prescribed ones or illegal drugs, since any substance that affects alertness or reaction time is a hazard behind the wheel regardless of whether a doctor prescribed it.
Sign 505 marks a stop for public bus transport, while sign 506 marks a stop for a public tramway, so the two signs distinguish between the two different modes of public transit.
In the vehicle diagram, the number 14 marks the measurement spanning from the center of the front axle to the center of the rear axle, which is exactly what 'wheelbase' means.
As with the general definition elsewhere in the law, a 'commercial vehicle' is simply a motor vehicle used or designed to transport goods.

Freight handling, arranging, loading, and unloading is lawfully counted as driving hours under the work-hours regulation, since it's a required part of a commercial driver's job and contributes to the same fatigue that driving-hour limits are meant to manage.

The controller of the vehicle is legally responsible for not letting the driver exceed the statutory work hours, since it's the controller who assigns routes and schedules that could otherwise push a driver into unsafe, fatigued driving.
The correct way to drive downhill is to stay in one of the gears throughout the descent, using engine braking to help control speed rather than coasting in neutral or riding the brakes continuously.

The speed retarder must be used going downhill whenever a 'dangerous descent' sign is posted, since that sign specifically flags a slope steep or long enough that the regular service brakes alone risk overheating.

Yes, an appropriate lower gear must be used on every steep descent, since engine braking through a low gear is what prevents the service brakes from overheating and losing effectiveness on a long downhill.

Stopping on a freeway is prohibited except on the hard shoulder, and only when the vehicle has broken down and genuinely cannot continue driving, since a freeway's high speeds make any other roadside stop extremely dangerous.

A 'path' is legally defined as any part of a road that is not the roadway itself and is designated for specific users, a broader definition covering pedestrian paths, bike paths, or other special-use lanes.

In a vehicle 220 cm wide, the extremity (width) side lights must be turned on during lighting-up time, since that width is well above the 210 cm threshold at which these lights become mandatory for marking the vehicle's full width in the dark.
